reconstructed_words.lxx_word: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ θεὸς πρὸς Μωυσῆν
reconstructed_words.reasoning: Standard LXX rendering of the wayyiqtol speech formula. καὶ εἶπεν = ויאמר, ὁ θεός = אלהים, πρὸς + accusative regularly translates אל with verbs of speaking in the Pentateuch.

The translator interprets rather than literally renders the idem-per-idem formula. ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν ('I am the One who is') is a philosophically inflected paraphrase of אהיה אשר אהיה, treating the second אהיה participially. Wevers (Notes on Exodus, ad loc.) sees no different Vorlage but a hellenizing exegesis.

alternatives.note: Highly unlikely retroversion; no textual support.

reconstructed_words.reasoning: Routine equivalence for the wayyiqtol of אמר.
οὕτως consistently renders כה in the Pentateuch; future ἐρεῖς for yiqtol תאמר is standard messenger-formula equivalence.
Dative without preposition rendering ל + construct בני ישראל is the formulaic LXX pattern throughout Exodus.

The translator renders the divine self-designation אהיה with a present participle ὁ ὤν, consistent with his earlier interpretive choice in v. 14a. There is no need to posit a different Vorlage; this is theological/philosophical translation technique (cf. Pietersma, NETS Exodus).

alternatives.note: Unattested and unlikely; LXX participle reflects exegesis of אהיה.

reconstructed_words.reasoning: ἀποστέλλω is the default equivalent for שלח (qal); the perfect ἀπέσταλκεν renders qatal with 1cs object suffix.
πρός + accusative regularly renders אל + 2mp suffix after verbs of sending.

summary_technical: The Vorlage of LXX Exodus 3:14 is essentially identical to MT; no variant reading need be posited. The notable divergence — ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν / ὁ ὤν for אהיה אשר אהיה / אהיה — reflects interpretive translation technique (an ontological reading of the divine name) rather than a different Hebrew text. No DSS witness preserves this verse to adjudicate, but the consonantal reconstruction is secure.
summary_plain: The Greek translator almost certainly had a Hebrew text identical to the Masoretic Text. The famous 'I am the One who is' is the translator's philosophical interpretation of the Hebrew 'I will be who I will be,' not evidence of a different Hebrew original.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Ontological Rendering of the Divine Name
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most consequential feature of LXX Exod 3:14 is exegetical, not text-critical: the translator construes אהיה as a participle of being (ὁ ὤν), producing the first explicit ontological reading of YHWH's self-disclosure. This is translation technique, not a lost Vorlage — there is no plausible Hebrew (e.g. ההוה) behind ὁ ὤν, and positing one would be speculation against the grain of LXX-Exodus's otherwise close adherence to a proto-MT consonantal text.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The Greek 'the One who is' is the translator's theological interpretation, not a sign that he had a different Hebrew text. This single rendering shaped centuries of Jewish and Christian thought about God's being.
